claims.text: Introducing a gradient or heterostructured microstructure can concurrently improve strength and ductility.
A nanostructured surface or layer over a coarser-grained interior is a gradient microstructure capable of producing concurrent strength–ductility improvement.
Coarse-grained regions maintain ductility through strain partitioning and back-stress hardening.
Surface severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing can create a nanostructured surface layer on a microcrystalline core.
Controlled temperature and strain rate can produce a well-defined grain-size gradient without cracks or undesirable phases.
The engineered gradient microstructure provides varying grain sizes across the material cross-section.
Nanostructured regions increase strength through Hall–Petch fine-grain strengthening.
Coarser-grained regions generate back stresses that delay necking.
Strain partitioning between fine- and coarse-grained regions improves both strength and ductility.
A gradient-microstructured material will exhibit higher yield strength than its homogeneous counterpart.
A gradient-microstructured material will maintain or increase ductility relative to its homogeneous counterpart.
A sufficiently pronounced difference in microstructural scales is required for simultaneous strength and ductility improvements.
Processing-induced defects can prevent simultaneous strength and ductility improvements.
The magnitude of improvement varies with alloy composition, processing parameters, and the degree of the gradient.
